entries.test: Musk's dated AI predictions and their outcomes establish his historical record, while worldwide humanoid robot and human population counts in 2040 test the prediction Marcus rejects.
entries.note: Marcus is quoting his own comments. The historical component is assessable now; the 2040 component remains outstanding.

entries.test: Public humanoid robot prices, affordability and demand surveys, and worldwide robot and car counts would test affordability, demand, and the six-to-one ratio.
Reported cumulative humanoid robot sales would show whether sales reach roughly 10 billion units in the nearish term.
entries.note: The emphatic dismissal commits to a negative forecast. 'Nearish term' supplies no fixed deadline.

entries.test: Public demonstrations and independent operational evaluations available by October 2024 would establish whether any humanoid robot safely and reliably performed a broad range of useful tasks.
entries.note: An independently demonstrated qualifying robot would refute the claim.

entries.test: OpenAI's published comparative performance results for o1 and GPT-4 would show whether they support a hundredfold improvement.
entries.note: Marcus says OpenAI's data do not support the comparison. The normalization adds a categorical contradiction of the annual improvement claim.
Potential bottlenecks express possible constraints, not a firm prediction that they will limit progress. The omission from Musk's presentation is separately checkable.

entries.test: Public capability evaluations by October 30, 2026 would show whether AI can perform every task a human can perform, with any demonstrated remaining inability refuting that universal capability.
entries.note: The dismissal and standing bet convey a firm negative prediction. The outer two-year deadline is two days after evaluation.

entries.test: Son's presentation and supporting materials would show whether the 10,000-fold intelligence figure has a defined metric and evidential derivation.
entries.note: 'Pure hype' is evaluative, but the assertion that the number lacks a defined meaning has a factual core.
The aphorism targets unsupported numerical predictions. The normalization broadens it to numerical AI predictions generally.
He gives no shared standard for attainable predictive precision or certainty. A forecast happening to prove accurate would not establish that its precision was justified.

The source says even believing in infinite scaling would not yield exact knowledge; the normalization substitutes scaling actually being unlimited. 'Any certainty' has no agreed evidential threshold here.
This is a recommendation about how audiences should treat the predictions.
Being lied to alleges knowing deception; being misled into thinking something instead asserts an audience effect. The source's allegation depends on the speakers' private knowledge or intent.
The normalization drops 'so many,' generalizing the claim to investors as a class. Fee arrangements are public-testable, but the asserted reason investors love these stories concerns private motives.

entries.test: Power-demand studies, utility fuel and generation plans, and fossil-fuel export revenue data would establish whether generative AI demand sustains fossil-fuel consumption and benefits oil-rich countries.
entries.note: The reliability clause says the asserted energy-demand effect does not depend on GenAI becoming reliable.

entries.test: Public media coverage and subsequent investor attention, fundraising, and valuation data could establish whether publicity for these claims increases AI investment enthusiasm.
entries.note: The surrounding discussion supplies a plain reading of 'drives up the whole thing' as amplifying the investment cycle.
